description: We are the Intersolvers: not just a team name, but our mission. Six people from five countries and different fields (design, storytelling, video, programming, project management, quality assurance, marketing), united by curiosity. We believe NASA’s open data should be easy for everyone to understand and use. For the Martian Map challenge, we turn real Mars data into a clear, interactive map that helps explorers move safely, because science is strongest when accurate and told as a story.
summary:
Our project combines an interactive terrain-mapping and route-planning platform with a tactical forearm wearable display concept to support astronaut EVA (Extravehicular Activity) planning at Murray Buttes, Gale Crater, Mars. Its web application serves both technical users, such as GIS professionals and mission planners, and general audiences interested in planetary exploration, balancing geospatial analysis with accessible public engagement without requiring hand-scanning hardware.

Integrating 1-meter resolution NASA/USGS datasets (MSL Gale DEM and HiRISE optical imagery), the platform evaluates a 498 × 499 meter grid and calculates four path strategies: shortest distance, roughness-avoidance, geological butte-avoidance, and our recommended minimum-energy route, while blocking steps steeper than an experimental 24° slope limit. Crucially, it handles data gaps transparently: across a suspicious DEM artifact line of 1,553 cells, 1,550 cells are reconstructed via interpolation so routes can cross safely while instantly triggering automated ambiguity warnings and crossing distances. Every route also undergoes Monte Carlo simulations to test energy sensitivity against elevation errors. Additionally, our conceptual AI Guide mockup (J.I.M) helps ordinary users explore the map easily without deep technical knowledge and educates aspiring astronauts through interactive Q&A inspired by historic missions like Apollo 13.
details:
🚀 What It Does and How It Works Our project presents an interactive terrain-mapping and route-planning platform alongside a conceptual tactical forearm wearable display designed to support astronaut navigation during EVAs. Inspired by a lightweight, detachable band worn on the forearm, the wearable concept illustrates how essential terrain and route information could be accessed during exploration without modifying the spacesuit. Our interactive web application demonstrates the platform's mapping and route-planning capabilities, while a visual wearable mockup illustrates its potential real-world application.

🗺️ Interactive Terrain & Replay Simulation Operating on a 498 × 499 meter grid of Gale Crater mapped at 1 meter per cell, the interface allows users to select a journey, inspect terrain rated as Go, Caution, or No-go, and compare routes across distance, estimated energy, slope, roughness, and geology. An astronaut replay feature walks each route with a dynamic color-changing ribbon matching the terrain under the boots.

🛰️ Data Processing & Routing Engine Under the hood, our platform merges the MSL Gale 1-meter DEM, HiRISE 0.25 m/pixel orthoimagery, and mapped geological buttes from Zenodo. Slope and roughness are mathematically derived from the DEM, while surface brightness and texture are extracted from HiRISE. THEMIS thermal inertia was evaluated as an exploratory layer but excluded from routing calculations as it negligibly affected path selection. A custom routing script evaluates step-by-step energy expenditure using elevation changes, enforcing a strict experimental cutoff for movements exceeding ~24°. It outputs four route options: Shortest Distance, Avoid Roughest 10%, Avoid Buttes (noting that avoiding buttes does not automatically guarantee avoiding isolated rocks), and Minimum Energy, our recommended option.

⚠️ Artifact Handling, Risk Analysis & AI Guide To resolve a data seam containing 1,553 suspect cells, we reconstructed 1,550 cells via interpolation. Routes are permitted to cross this zone, but the app automatically flags a warning with coordinates and crossing distance because the elevations are estimated rather than direct measurements. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations test route energy sensitivity against potential elevation errors. Drawing thematic inspiration from the systematic, calm, step-by-step problem-solving spirit of historic space missions like Apollo 13, we also designed an AI Guide presented as a standalone visual mockup interface rather than a live integrated backend feature, highlighting its high-value potential within the hackathon timeframe.

🎯 Benefits and Intended Impact Following a strategic 70% B2B / 30% B2C split, our project combines a high-precision GIS decision-support tool for space agencies, researchers, and astronauts (70%) with an intuitive, educational, and public-friendly experience (30%). Rather than giving crews a blind black-box path, comparing four strategies side by side clearly shows why the minimum-energy route outperforms a straight line across rough terrain, while automated artifact warnings and Monte Carlo simulations ensure honest uncertainty management. Meanwhile, our AI Guide concept bridges complex GIS data for the general public, enabling ordinary users to explore the map seamlessly without deep technical expertise and allowing students and aspiring astronauts to ask educational questions (such as inquiring about Apollo 13 mission history) to foster space science engagement.

💻 Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used We used Python to process planetary datasets, derive slope and roughness grids, interpolate the DEM artifact, calculate the four routing paths, and run Monte Carlo sensitivity simulations. Our web application and simulation were built using React and Vite as a serverless, lightweight static site, with the map interface custom-drawn onto an HTML5 Canvas component to ensure smooth panning, zooming, and real-time cursor/pin inspection. The app consumes pre-processed binary elevation/slope grids and a structured meta.json file generated by backend scripts for rapid browser performance, featuring modular views for layer controls, journey replays, elevation profiles, route comparison tables, risk matrices, and a downloadable route summary card. The hardware concept is designed for an adjustable strap-on forearm tactical display (supported by visual mockups of the wearable unit and AI Guide), integrating NASA/USGS MSL Gale 1 m DEM, HiRISE 0.25 m imagery, and Zenodo geological butte data.

💡 What Makes Our Project Creative Instead of a broad regional or global planetary map, we built a hyperlocal 1-meter view tailored specifically for a single astronaut walk. Framing a browser-based GIS simulation as a hands-free forearm tactical band paired with an Apollo 13-inspired educational AI Guide mockup merges practical astronaut ergonomics with compelling public storytelling. Most importantly, we prioritize radical data transparency through a dedicated Trust tab that clearly labels every layer as measured, derived, or modelled, alongside open disclosures of experimental thresholds and operational limits.

🛡️ Factors Considered Our team accounted for terrain elevation changes (walking energy), steepness (the experimental ~24° movement cutoff), local surface roughness, and mapped geological buttes. We prioritized data integrity by reconstructing the 1,553-cell DEM seam via 1,550 interpolated cells while explicitly warning users upon crossing, testing energy sensitivity with Monte Carlo simulations, and responsibly excluding THEMIS thermal inertia after testing proved its impact on routing was negligible. Finally, we maintained strict scientific honesty by clarifying that a Go rating means staying within our model's experimental limits rather than a certified astronaut safety guarantee.
